why_here: It evolved in the high-altitude lake system of the Valley of Mexico, and the Xochimilco canals are the last remnant of that ancient lake water.
fun_fact: Axolotls usually never undergo metamorphosis, keeping their feathery external gills and aquatic life as adults.
clue: It usually never grows up: adults keep feathery gills and live in the canals of a high lake.

why_here: It has been trapped in a single water-filled limestone cavern since the region dried out, and it breeds on one small sunlit rock shelf near the surface.
fun_fact: Its whole wild range is a single pool, often called the smallest range of any vertebrate on Earth.
clue: Its whole wild range is one pool in a desert cave, often called the smallest of any vertebrate.

why_here: Sloths on this small island were cut off from the mainland by rising seas and shrank in size over thousands of years of isolation.
fun_fact: Its entire world sits on an island of only about 4 square kilometres, and many live in red mangroves along the shore.
clue: Shrunk by isolation, it lives on an island of about 4 square km, often in red mangroves.

place: Ilha da Queimada Grande (Snake Island), Brazil
why_here: Rising sea levels isolated its ancestors on a small offshore island with no ground prey, so it adapted to hunting migratory birds.
fun_fact: Its venom is reported to be several times more potent than that of its mainland relative, the jararaca.
clue: With no ground prey on its tiny island, this viper ambushes migrating birds instead.

place: Upper Gulf of California near San Felipe, Mexico
why_here: This porpoise is confined to the warm, shallow, murky waters at the very northern end of the Gulf of California.
fun_fact: It is the world's most endangered marine mammal; 2025 surveys identified only around 7 to 10 individuals.
clue: The world's smallest porpoise. Only about 10 are left, in warm, murky water at a sea's far end.

place: Mountains of central Vancouver Island, British Columbia
why_here: It descends from marmots isolated on Vancouver Island's subalpine meadows after the last ice age.
fun_fact: Its chocolate-brown coat with a white nose patch sets it apart from every other marmot.
clue: Chocolate-brown with a white nose patch, it whistles from subalpine meadows on a big island.

why_here: Glaciers and lowland forest cut its meadows off from other marmots, leaving it isolated on the Olympic Peninsula's peaks.
fun_fact: Schoolchildren campaigned for years to get it named Washington's official endemic mammal in 2009.
clue: Glaciers stranded it on peak meadows; kids campaigned for years to make it a state emblem.

place: Santa Cruz Island, Channel Islands, California
why_here: Its ancestors reached a single Channel Island and have evolved there in isolation for about a million years.
fun_fact: It is the only land bird in the continental US that lives on just one island.
clue: Bigger and bluer than its mainland kin, it buries acorns on one hilly isle, alone for ages.

place: Cypress Point and Point Lobos, Monterey Peninsula, California
why_here: It is a relict of cooler times that survives only on two foggy headlands near Carmel.
fun_fact: Though planted worldwide, its entire native range is just two small coastal groves.
clue: Planted worldwide, yet wild only in two small groves on foggy, windswept headlands.

why_here: It depends on high-altitude bunchgrass meadows that exist only on a few volcanoes southeast of Mexico City.
fun_fact: Like pikas, and unlike other rabbits, it gives high-pitched calls to warn others of danger.
clue: A tiny, short-eared rabbit of high bunchgrass meadows that squeaks alarm calls like a pika.

why_here: Raccoons isolated on Cozumel evolved into a separate, much smaller species.
fun_fact: They have been seen rolling paper into balls as toys, a habit learned within family groups.
clue: A dwarf raccoon from a tropical island, seen rolling paper into balls to play with.

why_here: This hummingbird diverged from mainland relatives after colonizing Cozumel's forests.
fun_fact: Males sport a long, deeply forked tail that looks like a pair of scissors.
clue: A glittering hummingbird of island forests; males sport a long tail forked like scissors.

why_here: It evolved on a small Pacific island off Colombia, separated from mainland anoles.
fun_fact: Both males and females are entirely blue, a color that is extremely rare in lizards.
clue: Males and females alike are all blue, a rare colour for a lizard, on one small rainy island.

why_here: It needs the spring-fed gallery forests on the slopes of one plateau surrounded by dry caatinga.
fun_fact: It was not discovered until 1996, and part of its core breeding area lies inside a water theme park.
clue: Unknown until 1996, it needs spring-fed forest on a dry plateau; some breed in a water park.

why_here: It is tied to forest edges and scrub in one Andean valley system in northern Peru.
fun_fact: Males have only four tail feathers, two of which end in large racket-shaped discs they wave during courtship.
clue: Males have just four tail feathers, two tipped with rackets they wave in a mountain valley.

why_here: Its ancestors rafted to Grand Cayman and evolved in isolation in the island's dry shrubland.
fun_fact: It fell to fewer than 15 wild animals in 2003 and recovered to hundreds thanks to captive breeding.
clue: Fewer than 15 were left in the wild in 2003; breeding brought this dry-scrub lizard back.

why_here: Mongooses and development wiped it out elsewhere in Jamaica, leaving only the rugged dry limestone forest of Hellshire.
fun_fact: It was thought extinct until a hunter's dog chased one into a hollow log in 1990.
clue: Thought extinct until 1990, when a hunter's dog chased one into a log in dry limestone scrub.

why_here: This nearly flightless grebe evolved on a single high Andean lake and never leaves it.
fun_fact: It lives at over 4,000 m elevation and its fate depends on water levels controlled by a hydroelectric dam.
clue: Nearly flightless, it never leaves one lake over 4,000 m up, its level set by a hydro dam.

why_here: It is adapted to the cold, oxygen-poor water of the Titicaca basin and breathes mostly through its skin.
fun_fact: Its baggy, heavily folded skin increases surface area for absorbing oxygen; Cousteau's team filmed one 120 m deep.
clue: Baggy, folded skin soaks up oxygen in a cold, high lake; one was filmed 120 m deep.

place: Sulphur Mountain hot springs, Banff, Alberta
why_here: It lives only in the warm, sulphur-rich outflows of a handful of hot springs on one mountainside.
fun_fact: It thrives in water with so much hydrogen sulfide and so little oxygen that most animals could not survive.
clue: A tiny snail of warm, smelly hot-spring runoff on a mountainside, where little else survives.

place: Edwards Aquifer at San Marcos, Texas
why_here: It lives permanently in the dark, water-filled caves of one section of the Edwards Aquifer.
fun_fact: It has no functional eyes and no skin pigment, yet can regrow lost limbs and tail.
clue: Eyeless and ghost-white, it lives in flooded caves underground and can regrow lost limbs.

why_here: It depends on the constant cool spring water flowing out of the Barton Springs segment of the Edwards Aquifer.
fun_fact: Its species name comes from Austin's Save Our Springs ordinance.
clue: It keeps its frilly gills for life, in a single spring that stays cool all year round.

place: Coastal plain around Wilmington, North Carolina
why_here: It needs fire-maintained, nutrient-poor wet savannas found only in a small part of the Carolinas coastal plain.
fun_fact: A trap only snaps shut after two touches of its trigger hairs within about 20 seconds.
clue: A trap snaps only after two touches within about 20 seconds, in fire-swept, boggy savanna.

why_here: It is an ice-age relict that survived in the cool, shaded ravines along the Apalachicola River.
fun_fact: It was once so common that settlers cut its trunks into planks to build a riverside village.
clue: An ice-age relict conifer of cool, shady river ravines, once common enough to saw for planks.

place: Santa Lucia Mountains, Big Sur, California
why_here: It survives in fire-sheltered canyons and rocky slopes of the Big Sur coast range.
fun_fact: It is the rarest fir in North America, with spiky cones bristling with long needle-like bracts.
clue: The rarest fir on its continent, with spiky cones, in fire-sheltered canyons above the sea.

why_here: It is a relict of ice-age lakes and rivers that once filled the Owens Valley.
fun_fact: In 1969 the entire known population was carried to safety in two buckets.
clue: A relict of ice-age desert lakes. Its whole known population was once saved in two buckets.

place: Hawksbill, Stony Man and The Pinnacles, Shenandoah NP, Virginia
why_here: It clings to cool, rocky talus slopes on three peaks where competitors are scarce.
fun_fact: It has no aquatic larval stage; babies hatch from eggs on land as tiny salamanders.
clue: No water stage: babies hatch on land, on cool, rocky talus slopes of only three peaks.

why_here: It lives only in the spring-fed marshes of an isolated desert basin.
fun_fact: Unlike other box turtles it is mostly aquatic, spending about 90% of its time in water.
clue: Unlike its kin it is mostly aquatic, spending about 90% of its time in desert spring marsh.

why_here: Like the axolotl, it evolved to stay aquatic in a single high-altitude Mexican lake.
fun_fact: Nuns at a local convent have run a breeding program for it for years.
clue: Nuns at a convent breed this gilled, lifelong-aquatic amphibian from one high-altitude lake.

place: Isla Santa Catalina, Gulf of California, Mexico
why_here: It evolved in isolation on a single small desert island in the Gulf of California.
fun_fact: It is a rattlesnake with no rattle: the tail tip breaks off at each shed.
clue: No rattle here: the tail tip breaks off at each shed. It hunts on one small desert island.

why_here: It survives only in a fog-fed grove high on the north end of a remote Pacific island.
fun_fact: Its fruits are edible, which is where the name edulis comes from; goats nearly destroyed it before being removed.
clue: Its fruit is edible. It survives in a fog-fed grove on a remote island once ravaged by goats.

why_here: It evolved on a remote volcanic island far off Mexico's Pacific coast.
fun_fact: It was once placed in its own genus until DNA showed it is a true Mimus mockingbird.
clue: Once given a genus of its own until DNA showed its kin, it lives on a remote volcanic isle.

why_here: It is specialized for the mangrove forests of one small Caribbean island.
fun_fact: Its hatchlings are born dark rather than green, camouflaging them on the mangrove floor.
clue: Its hatchlings are dark, not green, hiding them on the mangrove floor of one small island.

why_here: Its ancestor reached this remote Pacific island and evolved there rather than in the Galápagos.
fun_fact: It is the only one of Darwin's finches that lives outside the Galápagos.
clue: Each bird picks its own speciality, nectar or insects or seeds, on one rainy, forested isle.

why_here: It lives only on the slopes of one volcano at the north end of Isabela.
fun_fact: Rangers first noticed the pink iguanas in 1986, but they were only named as a species in 2009.
clue: Pink with dark bands, it lives on just one volcanic slope, and was named a species in 2009.

why_here: Rich cold upwelling waters off the western Galápagos let it feed without flying, and there were no land predators to escape.
fun_fact: It is the only cormorant that cannot fly; its wings are about a third of the size needed.
clue: With wings about a third the size needed to fly, it dives in cold, rich seas off lava shores.

why_here: The cold Cromwell Current upwelling along the western islands lets a penguin survive on the equator.
fun_fact: It is the only penguin that naturally ventures into the Northern Hemisphere.
clue: A small penguin kept alive by a cold current welling up around hot, black lava-rock islands.

why_here: It depends on a couple of mangrove stands on Isabela after vanishing from Fernandina.
fun_fact: Fewer than about 40 adults remain, making it one of the rarest birds in the world.
clue: A tool user that pries grubs from dead wood with twigs, in a few mangrove stands on a volcano.

place: Champion and Gardner islets, off Floreana, Galápagos
why_here: Rats and cats wiped it out on Floreana, leaving it only on two tiny predator-free islets nearby.
fun_fact: Darwin collected it in 1835, and comparing it with other mockingbirds helped spark his ideas on evolution.
clue: Rats and cats wiped it from its home island, so it clings on two tiny, predator-free isles.

why_here: It evolved on the oldest, southernmost Galápagos island, isolated from other mockingbirds.
fun_fact: It is famously fearless and will hop onto tourists and peck at water bottles.
clue: Famously fearless, it hops onto tourists and pecks at water bottles on an old, dry island.

why_here: Each Galápagos island evolved its own tortoise; this saddle-backed one is native only to Española.
fun_fact: A male named Diego from the San Diego Zoo fathered a huge share of the hundreds of tortoises bred to save it.
clue: A saddle-backed giant saved by breeding: one male, Diego, fathered a huge share of the young.

why_here: It is adapted to the cold, dry, sun-blasted volcanic cinder above about 2,100 m on two Hawaiian volcanoes.
fun_fact: It flowers just once, after 20 to 90 years, sending up a giant stalk before dying.
clue: A silvery rosette on cold volcanic cinder above about 2,100 m. It blooms once, then dies.

place: Upper slopes of Mauna Kea, Hawaiʻi
why_here: It survives only in the high-elevation māmane forest on Mauna Kea, its key food source.
fun_fact: It feeds almost entirely on māmane seeds that are toxic to most other animals.
clue: It eats tree seeds that are toxic to most animals, in dry, high forest on a tall volcano.

why_here: It clings on in the last undisturbed wet forest on east Maui, above the elevation of disease-carrying mosquitoes.
fun_fact: It uses its heavy, parrot-like bill to rip apart bark and branches to find beetle larvae.
clue: Its heavy, hooked bill rips bark apart for beetle grubs in wet forest above mosquito country.

why_here: It survives in the cool, wet, remote streamside forests of Kauaʻi's high plateau.
fun_fact: Its call has been compared to a squeaky wheel that needs oil.
clue: Its call is likened to a squeaky wheel. It hides by streams in cool, wet forest on a plateau.

why_here: It is a relict Hawaiian honeycreeper surviving only on one tiny rocky island.
fun_fact: It eats seabird eggs as well as seeds, cracking them with its strong bill.
clue: On one tiny rocky island, it cracks seabird eggs as well as seeds with its strong bill.

why_here: This honeycreeper is native only to one small coral island in the remote Northwestern Hawaiian Islands.
fun_fact: When rabbits stripped Laysan bare, it survived by scavenging carrion and seabird eggs.
clue: When rabbits stripped its tiny coral island bare, it survived on carrion and seabird eggs.

why_here: It evolved on an isolated oceanic island 670 km off Chile.
fun_fact: Males and females look so different that they were once described as two separate species.
clue: Males and females look so unlike they were once named as two species. Home: one remote isle.

place: Cloud forest of Robinson Crusoe Island, Chile
why_here: This ancient plant lineage survives only in the cloud forest of one Juan Fernández island.
fun_fact: It is the only living member of its entire plant family, Lactoridaceae.
clue: The only living member of its entire plant family, hiding in misty forest on a remote isle.

why_here: It nests in sandstone cliffs and feeds on licuri palm nuts found in one patch of dry caatinga.
fun_fact: Its wild population was found only in 1978; before that it was known only from the pet trade.
clue: Known only from the pet trade until 1978, it nests in sandstone cliffs and eats palm nuts.

place: São João River basin, Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil
why_here: It survives in lowland Atlantic Forest fragments in a small part of Rio de Janeiro state.
fun_fact: Its blazing orange fur gets its color without any carotenoid pigments.
clue: Blazing orange fur with no carotenoid pigment, living in scraps of lowland coastal forest.

why_here: It lives only in low coastal forest around one island and adjacent mainland.
fun_fact: It was not described by science until 1990.
clue: Unknown to science until 1990, this black-faced monkey lives in low forest by the sea.

why_here: Its ancestors probably rafted across the Atlantic from Africa to this remote Brazilian archipelago.
fun_fact: It climbs mulungu trees to drink nectar and helps pollinate them.
clue: Its ancestors likely rafted over open sea from another continent. It sips nectar up in trees.

place: Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Colombia
why_here: It is restricted to the cloud forests of an isolated coastal mountain range.
fun_fact: It nests in dead wax palms.
clue: A green parrot of misty forest on an isolated coastal mountain range. It nests in dead palms.

why_here: It lives on the isolated summits of two table-top mountains, cut off from the lowlands below.
fun_fact: When threatened it curls into a ball and bounces down the rocks like a loose pebble.
clue: When threatened it curls into a ball and bounces down the rocks, atop table-top mountains.

why_here: It is restricted to high cloud-forest ridges on a few northwestern Ecuadorian volcanoes.
fun_fact: It is the official emblem of the city of Quito.
clue: A hummingbird with fluffy leg puffs, on misty ridges of a few volcanoes. A city's emblem.

why_here: It lives in dense, mossy cloud forest on a few ridges of the northern Peruvian Andes.
fun_fact: At about 13 cm long, it is one of the smallest owls in the world, with long whisker-like facial feathers.
clue: At about 13 cm, one of the smallest owls on Earth, hiding in dense, mossy forest on ridges.

place: Llanos de Moxos near Trinidad, Beni, Bolivia
why_here: It depends on palm-studded forest islands in the seasonally flooded savannas of Beni.
fun_fact: Fake-feather headdresses now replace traditional ones that once took many macaws' feathers.
clue: It needs palm-studded forest islands in flooded savanna; fake-feather headdresses spare it.

why_here: This flightless duck evolved on the Falklands' rocky coasts and cannot fly to leave.
fun_fact: It churns across the water using its wings like paddlewheels, which is how steamer ducks got their name.
clue: Flightless, it churns the water with its wings like paddlewheels along cold, rocky coasts.

why_here: It survives in the forested hills of Trinidad's Northern Range after vanishing from the lowlands.
fun_fact: Locals call it the pawi, and it is Trinidad and Tobago's only endemic bird.
clue: A big white-crowned forest bird, its country's only endemic bird, hanging on in wooded hills.

why_here: It evolved in the montane forests of one small volcanic Caribbean island.
fun_fact: The Soufrière Hills volcano eruptions starting in 1995 destroyed over half of its habitat.
clue: Volcanic eruptions starting in 1995 destroyed over half its forest home on one small island.

why_here: Each Lesser Antillean island evolved its own parrot; this one lives only in Saint Lucia's mountain forests.
fun_fact: It is the national bird and rebounded from about 150 birds in the late 1970s.
clue: A colourful parrot of mountain forest that rebounded from about 150 birds in the late 1970s.

why_here: It lives only in the high mountain rainforest of Dominica.
fun_fact: It appears on Dominica's national flag.
clue: A big purple-breasted parrot of high mountain rainforest that appears on its country's flag.

why_here: It is Saint Vincent's own parrot, restricted to the island's forested mountains.
fun_fact: Introduced armadillos threaten it by undermining the big nest trees it relies on.
clue: Introduced armadillos threaten it by undermining big nest trees in its forested mountains.

why_here: It is native only to Puerto Rico, and wild birds survive mainly in the Luquillo rainforest.
fun_fact: In 1975 only 13 remained in the wild.
clue: A green parrot that fell to 13 wild birds in 1975, now mostly in one wet mountain forest.

why_here: It is restricted to the dry coastal scrub forests of Grenada's west and southwest.
fun_fact: It has been Grenada's national bird since 1991.
clue: A shy ground dove of dry coastal scrub forest, its island nation's national bird since 1991.

why_here: Introduced mongooses wiped it out on Antigua, leaving it on tiny offshore islets.
fun_fact: It was once thought to number only about 50 snakes, making it among the world's rarest.
clue: A slender snake once down to about 50, saved on tiny islets after mongooses killed the rest.

why_here: It survives only on a flat limestone-and-coral island after disappearing from larger islands.
fun_fact: Fossils show it once lived on Puerto Rico and St. Thomas.
clue: Fossils show it once lived on bigger islands. Today it survives on one flat limestone isle.

why_here: It lives only in the sawgrass marshes of the Zapata Peninsula.
fun_fact: It is so distinct it is the only member of its genus, Ferminia.
clue: So distinct it has a genus all to itself, it skulks in sawgrass marsh within a vast swamp.

why_here: Hunting and habitat loss have confined it to the vast Zapata wetland.
fun_fact: It is the most land-loving of crocodiles and has long, strong legs for walking.
clue: The most land-loving crocodile, striding on long, strong legs through a vast tropical marsh.

why_here: It is Bermuda's only native land reptile, having reached the remote island long ago.
fun_fact: Hatchlings have bright blue tails.
clue: The only native land reptile on its remote island. Hatchlings flash bright blue tails.

why_here: It evolved on Barbados and is known only from patches of forest on the island.
fun_fact: At about 10 cm long and as thin as spaghetti, it is among the smallest snakes in the world.
clue: About 10 cm long and thin as spaghetti, one of the world's tiniest snakes, in island forest.

why_here: Socotra has been isolated from the mainland for millions of years, and this umbrella-shaped tree evolved there to capture moisture from monsoon mists on the island's highlands.
fun_fact: It is a monocot, a group that rarely grows thick trunks, yet it undergoes secondary growth and even shows ring-like zones in its wood.
clue: Its umbrella-shaped crown catches monsoon mist on the highlands of a long-isolated island.

why_here: It evolved in isolation on Socotra's dry lowlands; aside from a few trees on neighbouring Samhah it grows nowhere else.
fun_fact: It is the only member of the cucumber and pumpkin family that grows as a tree.
clue: The only tree in the pumpkin family, with a fat trunk, on a remote island's dry lowlands.

why_here: An island lineage that diverged from mainland red-winged starlings after reaching remote Socotra.
fun_fact: It nests in hollow dragon's blood tree branches and spreads the tree's seeds by eating its berries.
clue: It nests in hollows of umbrella-shaped trees and spreads their seeds by eating the berries.

why_here: A buzzard population that became isolated on Socotra's ravines and plateaus and evolved into its own species.
fun_fact: Scientists knew of it for over 110 years before formally recognising it as a separate species in 2010.
clue: Known for over 110 years before being named a species in 2010. It hunts arid island ravines.

why_here: Its ancestors reached Socotra and, cut off from the mainland, became a distinct island species.
fun_fact: Its two closest relatives live on the Arabian and Somali mainlands and were once lumped with it as one species.
clue: A stout-billed seed-eater of a dry, remote island. Its two closest kin live on mainlands.

why_here: Like much of Socotra's wildlife, this tarantula evolved in isolation on the island and is found nowhere else.
fun_fact: Unusually for tarantulas it lives communally, and mothers defend their egg sacs and young from intruders.
clue: Unlike most tarantulas it lives in colonies, and mothers guard their young. Home: an arid isle.

why_here: A falcon that evolved on Mauritius and now survives in the island's last native forests and gorges in the southwest.
fun_fact: In the 1970s only four or five wild birds remained, making it arguably the rarest bird on Earth; it is now Mauritius's national bird.
clue: In the 1970s only four or five were left in the wild. It hunts geckos in steep island forest.

why_here: It evolved on Mauritius and survives in the remaining native forest of Black River Gorges plus the offshore islet Île aux Aigrettes.
fun_fact: It is the only Mascarene pigeon that did not go extinct, despite falling to about 10 birds in 1991.
clue: Its island chain's last surviving native pigeon, it fell to about 10 wild birds in 1991.

why_here: The last surviving native Mascarene parrot, it clings on in about 40 km2 of native forest in southwest Mauritius.
fun_fact: It is named after Echo, the nymph of Greek myth.
clue: Named after a nymph of myth, it is the last native parrot on its chain of volcanic islands.

why_here: This tiny nectar-feeder evolved on Mauritius and now occupies only about 25 km2 of upland forest.
fun_fact: Hand-reared chicks in its rescue programme need a small feed roughly every forty minutes.
clue: A tiny nectar-feeder squeezed into about 25 km2 of misty upland forest on a volcanic island.

why_here: A weaver that evolved on Mauritius and occurs nowhere else.
fun_fact: Conservationists take eggs to hatch in captivity, prompting wild pairs to lay a second clutch and effectively double their output.
clue: A red weaver. Taking eggs to hatch in captivity makes wild pairs lay again, doubling output.

why_here: Once found on Mauritius and nearby islets, it survived only on rat-free Round Island after introduced animals wiped it out elsewhere.
fun_fact: Its skin changes colour over a day, dark when resting by day and paler at night when it hunts.
clue: Dark by day, it turns paler at night to hunt, on a rat-free islet of eroded volcanic rock.

why_here: It once lived across Mauritius, but since the 1800s it has survived only on Round Island, beyond the reach of rats and other introduced predators.
fun_fact: If grabbed it can shed its long tail to escape, then regrow it.
clue: A big lizard that can shed and regrow its tail, now found only on a rat-free volcanic islet.

why_here: Its natural wild range is just tiny Round Island off Mauritius, though it is now planted in gardens across the tropics.
fun_fact: Despite its swollen bottle-shaped trunk, it does not actually store water.
clue: Its swollen trunk stores no water. Gardens grow it widely, but wild ones cling to one islet.

why_here: A fruit bat that reached remote Rodrigues and evolved there; the island is its only home.
fun_fact: In captivity a dominant male gathers a harem of up to ten females.
clue: A golden-maned fruit bat of a remote, cyclone-prone island. A top male may keep ten mates.

why_here: It evolved on isolated Rodrigues and lives nowhere else.
fun_fact: It fell to just 5 or 6 pairs in 1968 but recovered to around a thousand birds through reforestation.
clue: Down to 5 or 6 pairs in 1968, it rebounded to about a thousand as its island was replanted.

why_here: A reed warbler lineage that colonised Rodrigues and became a separate island species.
fun_fact: Feared extinct in the 1960s, it was rediscovered in the 1970s.
clue: Feared extinct in the 1960s, it was found again a decade later on a small, remote island.

why_here: It is confined to about 16 km2 of native mountain forest in northern Réunion, above Saint-Denis.
fun_fact: Its locals' name 'tuit-tuit' imitates its whistled call.
clue: Locals name it after its whistled call. It lives in about 16 km2 of misty volcanic forest.

why_here: A harrier that evolved on Réunion; it is the island's only native breeding bird of prey.
fun_fact: Islanders call it the 'papangue'.
clue: Its island's only native breeding bird of prey, gliding low over steep volcanic slopes.

why_here: This palm grows wild only on Praslin and neighbouring Curieuse in the granitic Seychelles.
fun_fact: It has the largest seed of any plant, up to 25 kg; sailors once believed it grew on a tree under the sea.
clue: This palm has the largest seed of any plant, up to 25 kg. Sailors thought it grew undersea.

why_here: It breeds only on Praslin, centred on the palm forest of Vallée de Mai.
fun_fact: It is the national bird of the Seychelles.
clue: A dull brown-grey parrot that breeds only in the palm forest of one granite island.

why_here: It survives only in the coastal forest of La Digue, centred on the Veuve Nature Reserve.
fun_fact: Locally called 'veuve' (widow) for the male's black plumage, it gave its name to an Air Seychelles jet.
clue: Males are glossy black with long tail streamers, in coastal forest on a small granite isle.

why_here: An ancient lineage that survives only on exposed granite slopes of Mahé, in four small populations.
fun_fact: It was believed extinct until a few trees were found in the 1970s; its open fruit looks like a jellyfish.
clue: Thought extinct until a few turned up in the 1970s, it clings to bare granite island slopes.

why_here: A small falcon that evolved in the granitic Seychelles, breeding mainly on Mahé and a few nearby islands.
fun_fact: Its breeding territory of about 40 hectares is said to be the smallest of any bird of prey.
clue: Its territory of about 40 hectares may be the smallest of any bird of prey, on granite isles.

why_here: Its family has been isolated on the granitic Seychelles since they split from India; it lives only on Mahé, Silhouette and Praslin.
fun_fact: After the eggs hatch, a parent carries the tadpoles around on its back.
clue: A tiny frog whose parent carries the tadpoles on its back, in damp forest on granite islands.

why_here: Once widespread in the granitic Seychelles, it survived only on Frégate before being moved to a few other nearby islands.
fun_fact: It appears on the Seychelles 25-rupee banknote.
clue: A black-and-white songbird that once clung on to a single small granite island.

why_here: Aldabra's remoteness and lack of settlers spared it from the hunting that wiped out other Indian Ocean giant tortoises.
fun_fact: Aldabra holds about 180,000 of them; one called Adwaita reportedly lived to around 255.
clue: About 180,000 roam one remote ring of coral. One is said to have lived to around 255.

why_here: A huge fruit bat that evolved on the Comoros and lives only in the montane forests of Anjouan and Mohéli.
fun_fact: Pups are born furred with eyes open and grip their mothers with big feet straight away.
clue: One of the biggest fruit bats, roosting in mountain forest on two volcanic islands.

why_here: It lives only in the forest and heath on the slopes of the active volcano Mount Karthala.
fun_fact: Almost nothing is known about it, but it readily approaches imitations of its call.
clue: Almost nothing is known about it, but it flies in to imitations of its call on a live volcano.

why_here: Endemic to the forest on Mount Karthala's slopes on Grande Comore.
fun_fact: Its crown feathers look like the beginnings of a crest, and its plumage is unusually soft and fluffy.
clue: Soft, fluffy plumage and a hint of a crest, in forest on an active island volcano's slopes.

why_here: It lives only in a narrow strip of northeastern rainforest between Maroantsetra and the Marojejy massif.
fun_fact: Males scent-mark trees with their chests, leaving a brown stain that is the only easy way to tell them from females.
clue: A pure white leaper of humid mountain rainforest. Males scent-mark trees with their chests.

why_here: It is hemmed into forest fragments around Daraina by the Manambato and Loky rivers.
fun_fact: It has been seen leaving the trees to cross over 200 m of open grassland between forest patches.
clue: Hemmed in by rivers, it has been seen crossing over 200 m of open grassland between woods.

why_here: Its range is boxed in between the Irodo and Loky rivers at Madagascar's northern tip.
fun_fact: Local Antankarana legend says the species descends from a hero called Radjako.
clue: An all-black leaper boxed into dry tropical forest between two rivers. A very rare primate.

why_here: It is restricted to forest between the Andranomalaza and Maevarano rivers in northwestern Madagascar.
fun_fact: Both sexes have blue eyes, a rarity among primates other than humans.
clue: Males are black and females reddish-tan, in tropical forest squeezed between two rivers.

why_here: It lives only in the papyrus and reed beds around Madagascar's largest lake.
fun_fact: It is the only primate adapted to living in papyrus, and unlike its relatives it eats no bamboo.
clue: The only primate adapted to papyrus, in reed beds round a big highland lake. It eats no bamboo.

why_here: It survives in rainforest from Ranomafana to Andringitra, where its giant-bamboo food plant grows.
fun_fact: It eats about 500 g of bamboo a day, enough cyanide to kill a dozen animals its size.
clue: It eats about 500 g of bamboo a day, enough cyanide to kill a dozen animals its size.

why_here: This bright frog is confined to a few swampy forest sites centred on Moramanga in eastern Madagascar.
fun_fact: Its vivid orange skin warns predators of toxins it gets from its insect diet.
clue: Its warning colours come from toxins in the insects it eats. It lives in a few swampy woods.

why_here: Once thought extinct, its only wild birds live on the northern highland lakes of Sofia and nearby Matsaborimena.
fun_fact: It went unnoticed for years partly because observers mistook it for the ferruginous duck.
clue: Once thought extinct, its last wild birds dive for food on a few remote highland lakes.

why_here: The whole wild population grows on a few hectares of limestone hillside in Analalava District.
fun_fact: Nicknamed the 'suicide palm', it grows for decades, flowers once in a giant display, and then dies.
clue: It grows for decades, flowers once in a giant display, then dies. All wild ones share a hill.

why_here: It is known only from montane rainforest on the Sorata massif in northern Madagascar.
fun_fact: Adult males are about 22 mm long including the tail, possibly the smallest reptile in the world.
clue: Adult males are about 22 mm long with the tail, perhaps the world's smallest reptile.

why_here: Island dwarfing on one tiny islet off northern Madagascar produced this miniature chameleon.
fun_fact: It is small enough to stand on a match head, and adults sport bright orange tails.
clue: Small enough to stand on a match head, with an orange tail, on one tiny limestone islet.

why_here: Once across El Hierro, it survived only on an inaccessible cliff where introduced cats and humans could not reach it.
fun_fact: Females can store viable sperm for up to a year after mating.
clue: Females can store sperm for up to a year. It hung on only on a sheer cliff cats can't reach.

why_here: Each large Canary Island evolved its own giant lizard, and this one belongs to Gran Canaria.
fun_fact: At up to 80 cm, it is among the largest lizards in its family.
clue: Up to 80 cm long, a giant of its family. Each big isle in its volcanic group has its own.

why_here: It survives on two sheer cliffs above Valle Gran Rey, out of reach of feral cats.
fun_fact: Described from bones and presumed extinct, it was rediscovered alive in 1999 with just six individuals.
clue: Known only from bones, it was found alive in 1999 with six left, on two sheer volcanic cliffs.

why_here: A chaffinch that adapted to Tenerife's high Canary pine forests and became a separate species.
fun_fact: It is a natural symbol of Tenerife alongside the dragon tree.
clue: It cracks pine seeds in high pine forest on the flanks of a huge volcano, above the clouds.

why_here: It is restricted to a few pine forests in Gran Canaria's highlands, chiefly the Inagua reserve.
fun_fact: Unusually for a finch, it feeds its young mainly on insects.
clue: Unusually for a finch, it feeds its chicks mostly on insects, in a few highland pine woods.

why_here: It is adapted to the high volcanic slopes around Mount Teide.
fun_fact: It grows as a leaf rosette for a year, sends up a red flower spike up to 3 m tall, then dies.
clue: A leafy rosette sends up a red flower spike up to 3 m tall, then dies, on high volcanic slopes.

why_here: It is adapted to the arid ravines and rocky slopes of Fuerteventura and is found nowhere else.
fun_fact: Its call sounds like two pebbles being knocked together.
clue: Its call sounds like two pebbles knocked together, in arid ravines and rocky island slopes.

why_here: It depends on Madeira's ancient laurel forest, which survives mostly on the island's northern slopes.
fun_fact: Its name comes ultimately from the Latin for 'collar', after its silvery neck patch.
clue: A grey pigeon with a silvery neck patch that needs ancient evergreen forest on steep slopes.

why_here: A tiny kinglet that evolved in isolation on Madeira's mountain forests.
fun_fact: The 5-gram female may line her nest with up to 3,000 feathers.
clue: The 5 g female may line her nest with up to 3,000 feathers, in a remote isle's mountain forest.

why_here: It grows wild only in Madeira's central uplands at the edge of the laurel forest.
fun_fact: Though now a popular garden plant worldwide, it is absent from even the other islands of the Madeira group.
clue: Grown in gardens worldwide, its blue flower spikes grow wild only by a laurel forest's edge.

why_here: Once on several Cape Verde islands, it survived only on uninhabited Raso, free of introduced predators.
fun_fact: Males have long bills used in dominance contests rather than for digging.
clue: Males use long bills in dominance contests, on one tiny, dry, uninhabited volcanic island.

why_here: Plovers that reached this remote mid-Atlantic island stayed and became a resident species.
fun_fact: Called the wirebird for its thin legs, it is St Helena's national bird and appears on its flag.
clue: A thin-legged plover of one very remote island, where it is the national bird and on the flag.

why_here: It evolved on St Helena and was nearly wiped out by goats and timber cutting.
fun_fact: Only two wild plants were found, on a cliff; it is not a true ebony but a member of the mallow family.
clue: Not a true ebony but a mallow relative. Only two wild plants were found, on a sheer cliff.

why_here: Its ancestors flew to this predator-free 14 km2 island and then lost the ability to fly.
fun_fact: It is the world's smallest living flightless bird, and its genus name nods to Atlantis.
clue: The world's smallest living flightless bird, on a predator-free island of about 14 km2.

why_here: A nearly flightless moorhen that evolved on remote Gough Island in the South Atlantic.
fun_fact: It is named for polar explorer George Comer, who wrote its first description in 1888.
clue: It can barely fly, scuttling through tussock grass on a cold, windswept, remote island.

why_here: It evolved on the volcanic island of São Tomé and lives in its central forests.
fun_fact: It is the world's largest sunbird and the only species in its genus.
clue: The world's biggest sunbird, probing flowers in misty rainforest on an old tropical volcano.

why_here: It lives only in undisturbed lowland forest in the south of São Tomé.
fun_fact: When stressed its call has been rendered as 'walalalala'.
clue: A small forest ibis whose stressed call sounds like 'walalalala', in remote island rainforest.

why_here: A canary relative that evolved in São Tomé's forests and grew unusually large.
fun_fact: It is the biggest canary in its genus, about half again heavier than the runner-up.
clue: Heaviest in its seed-eater genus by about half, a hulking finch of volcanic island rainforest.

why_here: It survives only in two neighbouring cloud forests: the Virunga volcanoes and Bwindi Impenetrable Forest.
fun_fact: Each gorilla has a unique nose print used to identify individuals.
clue: Each has a unique nose print. It lives in two neighbouring cloud forests on volcanic slopes.

why_here: This wild goat is adapted to the cliffs of Ethiopia's Simien Mountains, its only home.
fun_fact: It often rears up on its hind legs to browse young shoots of giant heath.
clue: A wild goat that rears on its hind legs to browse giant heath, on sheer cliffs of a plateau.

why_here: It is confined to the high Afroalpine grasslands of the Bale Mountains, under 1,000 km2.
fun_fact: Its eyes sit high on its head like periscopes, and it is a key prey of Ethiopian wolves.
clue: Periscope eyes help it watch for wolves in high, chilly grassland covering under 1,000 km2.

why_here: It needs the cold, permanent mountain streams in a few ravines on Table Mountain.
fun_fact: Its tadpoles use a sucker-like mouth to climb wet vertical rock.
clue: Its tadpoles climb wet vertical rock with sucker mouths, in cold, year-round ravine streams.

why_here: It grows naturally mainly on Table Mountain's slopes, with a few small outlying stands nearby.
fun_fact: Its leaves are covered in silky hairs that make the whole tree shimmer silver.
clue: A protea relative with silky-haired leaves, growing mainly on the slopes of a peak by the sea.

why_here: It grows only in peaty mountain seeps of the Kogelberg and Kleinrivier mountains.
fun_fact: Its seeds can wait underground for 35 years for a fire to trigger germination.
clue: Its seeds can wait underground 35 years for a fire to wake them, in peaty mountain seeps.

why_here: It lives only in three brackish estuaries on South Africa's Garden Route.
fun_fact: It shifts colour with mood and surroundings, from pale green to almost black.
clue: It shifts colour with mood, from pale green to near black, in only three brackish estuaries.

why_here: It lives in the underground lake of a single dolomite cave, where it evolved for life in darkness.
fun_fact: It is pigmentless with tiny skin-covered eyes, and is the only known cavefish in mainland southern Africa.
clue: Pale and nearly blind, it swims in a pitch-dark underground lake inside one dolomite cave.

why_here: It is restricted to the high montane grasslands of the Nimba Range.
fun_fact: Instead of laying eggs, females give birth to fully formed toadlets.
clue: A toad that skips eggs: females give birth to tiny toadlets in high mountain grassland.

why_here: This conifer grows on the high plateaus of the isolated Mulanje Massif.
fun_fact: It is Malawi's national tree, and its timber resists termites and rot.
clue: A national tree with rot- and termite-proof timber, on the high plateaus of a lone massif.

why_here: It lives on screw-pine trees in about 8 km2 of lowland forest at the foot of the Uluguru Mountains.
fun_fact: Males can switch from dull grey to electric blue depending on mood and temperature.
clue: Males flash electric blue on screw pines in a lowland forest patch of only about 8 km2.

why_here: It is confined to the forests of the Udzungwa Mountains.
fun_fact: It eats soil, probably for minerals and to counter toxins in its leaf diet.
clue: A leaf-eating monkey that snacks on soil, likely for minerals, in tropical mountain forest.

why_here: Isolated on Zanzibar's main island when rising seas cut it off from the mainland.
fun_fact: Locals call it 'kima punju', meaning 'poison monkey', for its strong smell.
clue: Stranded on an island by rising seas, its strong smell earns it a 'poison monkey' nickname.

why_here: This fruit bat evolved on Pemba, an island long separated from the African coast by deep water.
fun_fact: With a wingspan of about 1.6 m, it is one of the largest fruit bats.
clue: A huge fruit bat with wings about 1.6 m across, on a tropical island cut off by deep water.

why_here: It lives in a narrow ribbon of riverside forest on the lower Tana floodplain in a dry region.
fun_fact: It eats clay and charcoal, likely to neutralise toxins in its leaves.
clue: It eats clay and charcoal to beat leaf toxins, in a thin ribbon of riverside forest.

why_here: It lives only in a few cloud-forest fragments on the isolated Taita Hills, totalling about 340 hectares.
fun_fact: It is named after zoologist Edmund Heller.
clue: A shy thrush of a few cloud-forest scraps, about 340 hectares in all, on isolated hills.

why_here: It survives in a few square kilometres of the Hula wetlands after the valley was drained in the 1950s.
fun_fact: Declared extinct in 1996, it was rediscovered in 2011 and turned out to be a 'living fossil' of an otherwise extinct genus.
clue: Declared extinct in 1996, this 'living fossil' frog resurfaced in a drained marsh in 2011.

why_here: It is found in just four streams in one catchment of the southern Zagros Mountains.
fun_fact: When its streams dry up, it retreats into oak woodland and waits out the dry season.
clue: It lives in just four mountain streams, and when they dry up it hides out in oak woodland.

why_here: It is the only fish able to live in highly alkaline Lake Van, spawning in the lake's freshwater inflows.
fun_fact: During its spring migration it leaps up streams like a salmon, and locals catch them mid-air in bags.
clue: The only fish in a vast soda lake. It leaps up streams to spawn and gets caught mid-air.

why_here: It is one of 11 cichlids that evolved inside this small isolated crater lake.
fun_fact: Barombi Mbo's cichlids are a textbook example of species splitting within a single lake.
clue: One of 11 cichlids that evolved in one small crater lake, a textbook case of speciation.

why_here: Rock-dwelling Malawi cichlids rarely cross open sand or deep water, so this one is confined to one stretch of the central western shore.
fun_fact: Females brood the eggs in their mouths for about three weeks.
clue: Rock-bound, it won't cross open sand. Mothers brood eggs in their mouths for about 3 weeks.

why_here: It grows only on the nutrient-poor ultramafic soils of Mount Kinabalu and neighbouring Mount Tambuyukon, at 1,500-2,650 m.
fun_fact: Its lower pitchers can hold about 3.5 litres of fluid and have been known to drown rats.
clue: Its giant pitchers hold about 3.5 litres and have drowned rats, on a tropical peak's slopes.

why_here: It lives only in the cool, wet high-elevation forest of Mount Kinabalu, at about 2,500-3,000 m.
fun_fact: It doesn't suck blood at all: it hunts and swallows Kinabalu's giant earthworms.
clue: A red leech that ignores blood and swallows giant earthworms in cool forest near 3,000 m.

place: Cat Ba Island, Ha Long Bay, Vietnam
why_here: This golden-headed monkey survives only on the limestone karst cliffs of a single island at the edge of Ha Long Bay.
fun_fact: The island has no rivers, and these langurs can cope with drinking salty water.
clue: A golden-headed monkey on limestone cliffs of a riverless island. It copes with salty water.

why_here: This isolated orangutan lineage survives only in about 1,000 km2 of upland forest south of Lake Toba.
fun_fact: Described only in 2017, it is the rarest great ape on Earth, with fewer than 800 left.
clue: Named only in 2017, it is the rarest great ape, with fewer than 800 left in upland forest.

why_here: Its entire population lives on one tiny volcanic island of about 7 km2 far out in the Andaman Sea.
fun_fact: It has the smallest range of any Asian hornbill - the whole species fits on an island you could walk across in an hour or two.
clue: The whole species lives on one tiny volcanic island of about 7 km2, far out at sea.

why_here: It is confined to the summit ridges of the Victoria massif, above about 1,450 m on ultramafic soils.
fun_fact: Named after David Attenborough, it was hyped as a rat-eater in 2009; insects are its usual prey, though a dead shrew was later found in one pitcher.
clue: A giant pitcher plant that mostly eats insects, rooted in metal-rich soil on tropical summits.

why_here: This dwarf buffalo evolved on Mindoro and now survives only in a few remote grasslands, mainly in Mounts Iglit-Baco.
fun_fact: It is the only wild cattle species found only in the Philippines.
clue: A small, stocky wild buffalo with short V-shaped horns, hiding in remote island grassland.

why_here: This ground dove is found only in the lowland forests of Mindoro Island.
fun_fact: It gets its name from a blood-red patch on its white chest that looks like a wound.
clue: A ground dove with a blood-red splash on its white chest, like a wound, in lowland forest.

why_here: This small deer lives only on the Calamian Islands north of Palawan.
fun_fact: Instead of leaping obstacles it barrels under them head-down, like a pig - hence its other name, hog deer.
clue: Rather than leap obstacles, this small island deer barrels under them head-down, like a pig.

why_here: A relict 'living fossil' rabbit, it survives only on Amami Oshima and Tokunoshima.
fun_fact: It is dark, short-eared and calls to other rabbits - unusual for a rabbit.
clue: A dark, short-eared 'living fossil' that calls to others, rare for a rabbit, on two islands.

why_here: This purple-and-chestnut jay lives only on Amami Oshima and tiny Kakeromajima.
fun_fact: Its numbers have rebounded since introduced mongooses were wiped out on Amami in 2024.
clue: A purple-and-chestnut jay, rebounding on its island since invasive mongooses were removed.

why_here: This nearly flightless rail lives only in the Yanbaru forests of northern Okinawa, a range of about 260 km2.
fun_fact: It was only described by science in 1981, despite living on a well-populated island.
clue: A nearly flightless rail on a busy subtropical island, yet unknown to science until 1981.

why_here: It depends on mature subtropical forest found only in the Yanbaru hills of northern Okinawa.
fun_fact: It is one of the rarest woodpeckers in the world, but was downlisted to Endangered in 2024 as its numbers stabilised.
clue: One of the world's rarest woodpeckers, needing old subtropical forest on an island's hills.

why_here: This wild cat is found only on Iriomote, a jungle-covered island of about 290 km2.
fun_fact: No other wild cat lives in a smaller area; it even swims and hunts crabs and frogs.
clue: No wild cat has a smaller range. It swims and hunts crabs and frogs on a jungle-clad island.

why_here: Once found across the Bonins, it now survives only on Hahajima and two islets nearby.
fun_fact: Its name 'familiare' means friendly - it was usually the first bird visitors met.
clue: Its Latin name means 'friendly': it was often the first bird visitors met on its islands.

why_here: Lake Biwa is one of the world's oldest lakes, and this catfish evolved there and nowhere else.
fun_fact: It can grow over a metre long - fitting for the country whose myths blame earthquakes on a giant catfish, Namazu.
clue: It can grow over a metre long, and evolved in one of the world's oldest lakes, nowhere else.

place: Qijiawan Creek, Shei-Pa National Park, Taiwan
why_here: Trapped in cold mountain streams after the last Ice Age, it survives only in the upper Dajia River basin.
fun_fact: It is the southernmost naturally occurring salmon in Asia - living in the subtropics.
clue: An Ice Age leftover stuck in cold mountain streams: a salmon living in the subtropics.

why_here: Once widespread in China, it now survives only in a patch of forest in Bawangling on Hainan Island.
fun_fact: Only a couple of dozen remain, making it perhaps the world's rarest primate.
clue: Only a couple of dozen remain, in one patch of island forest. Perhaps the rarest primate.

why_here: It split from its mainland relative about 1.4 million years ago, when Hainan was cut off from the mainland.
fun_fact: Males fan their tails to show off rows of shimmering eye-spots like a tiny peacock.
clue: Males fan tails of shimmering eye-spots, on an island cut off from the mainland long ago.

why_here: Its only confirmed home is the forests of the Fanjingshan mountain reserve in Guizhou.
fun_fact: Fewer than 400 remain, making it the rarest of China's snub-nosed monkeys.
clue: Fewer than 400 remain, all in the forests of a single misty mountain reserve.

why_here: This relic conifer survives in the wild only in a few mountain valleys where Hubei, Chongqing and Hunan meet.
fun_fact: Scientists knew it only from fossils and thought it extinct until living trees were found in the 1940s.
clue: Known only from fossils and thought extinct, until live trees turned up in remote valleys.

place: Trung Khanh, Cao Bang, Vietnam-China border
why_here: The last survivors cling to one small patch of karst forest straddling the Vietnam-China border.
fun_fact: Females perform rhythmic 'dances' that researchers think may be a form of non-violent competition.
clue: The last few cling to one patch of karst forest, where females 'dance' to compete.

place: Van Long Nature Reserve, Ninh Binh, Vietnam
why_here: It lives only on limestone karst hills in a roughly 6,000 km2 pocket of northern Vietnam.
fun_fact: Its white 'shorts' over a black body make it look like it is wearing bermudas.
clue: A black monkey with white fur 'shorts' like bermudas, clambering on limestone karst hills.

place: Khau Ca / Na Hang, northern Vietnam
why_here: Its last populations survive on forested karst hills in a few districts of northern Vietnam.
fun_fact: It was feared extinct until a group was rediscovered in Na Hang in the 1990s.
clue: Feared extinct until it was found again in the 1990s, it clings to forested limestone hills.

why_here: It lives only in high, wet forests of the Gaoligong range along the Myanmar-China border.
fun_fact: Locals say it sneezes when rain falls into its upturned nose, so it sits with its head between its knees in storms.
clue: Rain up its upturned nose makes it sneeze, so in storms it sits with its head tucked down.

why_here: This little fish evolved in Inle Lake, an isolated highland lake, and lives nowhere else.
fun_fact: It has almost no scales, and breeding males flash a red snout and tail.
clue: An almost scaleless fish of an isolated highland lake. Breeding males flash a red snout.

place: Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary, Arunachal Pradesh, India
why_here: This colourful babbler is known only from the hillsides of Eaglenest sanctuary in the eastern Himalaya.
fun_fact: It was named in 2006 without killing a single bird - scientists used feathers, photos and recordings instead.
clue: A colourful babbler named in 2006 without killing a single bird, on steep mountain slopes.

why_here: Once found along the Himalayan foothills, it now survives only in the tall grasslands of Manas and nearby reintroduction sites in Assam.
fun_fact: It's the world's smallest pig - adults weigh under 10 kg.
clue: The world's smallest pig, under 10 kg, rooting through tall grassland below high mountains.

place: Horton Plains, central highlands, Sri Lanka
why_here: It is confined to cool montane forests of Sri Lanka's central highlands.
fun_fact: When threatened it gapes to flash a bright orange mouth lining; males carry a soft 'horn' on their snout.
clue: Males wear a soft snout 'horn', and it flashes an orange mouth when scared, in cool forest.

why_here: It lives only on high talus slopes of a few Tian Shan ridges in Xinjiang.
fun_fact: Its teddy-bear face went viral when it was rephotographed in 2014, more than 20 years after its discovery.
clue: A teddy-bear-faced pika that went viral in 2014, living on high rocky slopes of cold ridges.

why_here: This ancient salamander lives only in cold mountain streams of the Dzungarian Alatau range.
fun_fact: It is a relict of a group that was once widespread across Asia.
clue: An ancient relict of a once-widespread group, hiding in cold, fast-flowing mountain streams.

place: Ujung Kulon National Park, West Java
why_here: Once found across Southeast Asia, its last wild population is in Ujung Kulon at Java's western tip.
fun_fact: Fewer than 100 exist, all in one park, and it is the least studied rhino on Earth.
clue: Fewer than 100 exist, all in one lowland rainforest park. The least studied rhino on Earth.

why_here: This snow-white starling is native only to northwestern Bali and its offshore islands.
fun_fact: It is Bali's only endemic vertebrate and appears on Indonesia's 200-rupiah coin.
clue: A snow-white starling with bare blue skin around its eyes, from dry monsoon forest by the sea.

why_here: This small deer lives only on Bawean, an isolated island in the Java Sea.
fun_fact: Unlike adults, its fawns are born spotted.
clue: Its fawns are born spotted, unlike the adults, on one small, isolated tropical island.

why_here: It lives only on Komodo, Rinca, western Flores and two tiny islets nearby.
fun_fact: Females can lay fertile eggs without a male, producing all-male babies.
clue: The world's largest lizard. Females can lay fertile eggs with no male, on dry, hilly isles.

place: Siau Island, Sangihe arc, North Sulawesi
why_here: This tiny primate lives only on Siau, a single small volcanic island north of Sulawesi.
fun_fact: Each of its eyes is about as big as its brain, and it can't move them, so it swivels its head instead.
clue: Each eye is about as big as its brain and can't move, so it turns its head. Home: one volcano.

why_here: Native only to the northeastern tip of Sulawesi, with Tangkoko holding its largest remaining population.
fun_fact: A macaque of this species named Naruto took the famous 'monkey selfie' that sparked a copyright battle.
clue: A black, punk-crested monkey. One of them snapped the famous 'monkey selfie'.

place: Togian Islands, Gulf of Tomini, Sulawesi
why_here: This 'pig-deer' evolved in isolation on the Togian Islands in the Gulf of Tomini.
fun_fact: Males grow upper tusks that pierce straight up through the snout and curve back toward the forehead.
clue: Males grow tusks that pierce up through the snout and curve back, on small tropical islands.

why_here: It has no floating larval stage, so it can't disperse far and stays around the Banggai archipelago.
fun_fact: Dads brood the eggs in their mouths for up to a month without eating.
clue: Dads brood the eggs in their mouths for up to a month without eating, in warm, shallow bays.

why_here: This pig-tailed macaque lives only on Siberut, the largest of the isolated Mentawai Islands off Sumatra.
fun_fact: It was long lumped with the macaque on nearby Pagai, but turned out to be a separate lineage.
clue: A pig-tailed monkey once lumped with its neighbour, now its own lineage on a rainforest isle.

why_here: Lake Ohrid is over a million years old, and this trout evolved in it and its outflow.
fun_fact: It appears on North Macedonia's 2-denar coin.
clue: It evolved in a deep, clear lake over a million years old, and in the river that drains it.

why_here: This trout evolved in Lake Garda and attempts to start it in other lakes have all failed.
fun_fact: It spawns deep in the lake, unlike most trout, which spawn in streams.
clue: Unlike most trout it spawns deep in its lake. Every bid to stock it elsewhere has failed.

why_here: It depends on Corsica's old mountain Corsican-pine forests and lives nowhere else.
fun_fact: It is the only bird species found only in France.
clue: A tiny nuthatch of old mountain pinewoods on a rugged isle, its country's only endemic bird.

why_here: Wiped out elsewhere on Mallorca, it survives in limestone gorges of the Serra de Tramuntana.
fun_fact: Scientists described it from fossils in 1977, then found it alive two years later. Males carry the eggs.
clue: Described from fossils in 1977, then found alive two years later. Males carry the eggs.

why_here: Wiped out from Mallorca and Menorca, it survives on surrounding predator-free islets and Cabrera.
fun_fact: It pollinates several Balearic plants that depend on it.
clue: It pollinates plants that depend on it, on small rocky isles with no predators.

why_here: A relic from warmer times, it survives only in shady limestone crevices on Mount Olympus.
fun_fact: Its relatives are mostly tropical African violets - it's a leftover from a time when Europe was much warmer.
clue: A relic of warmer times with mostly tropical kin, tucked in shady limestone crevices.

why_here: Forests of it once covered Sicily's mountains; the last wild trees survive in one valley of the Madonie.
fun_fact: Only about 27 mature trees remain in the wild.
clue: Only about 27 mature trees remain in the wild, all in one valley of an island's mountains.

why_here: This relic tree survives only in a damp gully in the Iblei Mountains of southeast Sicily.
fun_fact: The 200-odd wild plants may all be clones of a single tree.
clue: Its 200-odd wild plants grow in one damp island gully, and may all be clones of one tree.

why_here: It grows only in a few stands in the western Troodos Mountains, centred on Cedar Valley.
fun_fact: Its needles are much shorter than those of its cousin, the cedar of Lebanon.
clue: A cedar with unusually short needles, in a few stands in an island's mountain valleys.

why_here: It grows wild only on the limestone cliffs of the Rock of Gibraltar.
fun_fact: It was presumed extinct until it was rediscovered in the Upper Rock Nature Reserve in 1994.
clue: Presumed extinct, it was found again in 1994 clinging to sheer limestone cliffs.

why_here: This butterfly lives only on the high slopes of Andalusia's Sierra Nevada.
fun_fact: Males are bright sky-blue, while females are brown with orange spots.
clue: Males are sky-blue, females brown with orange spots. It flies in high summer on rocky peaks.

why_here: It nests only on a handful of high ledges in Madeira's central mountains (it forages widely at sea).
fun_fact: Thought extinct, it was rediscovered in 1969 when a shepherd recognised its call from a recording.
clue: Thought extinct until 1969, when a shepherd knew its call. It nests on high mountain ledges.

place: Pico da Vara, Sao Miguel, Azores
why_here: It is tied to the last native laurel forest at the eastern end of Sao Miguel.
fun_fact: It is one of Europe's rarest birds, living in about 6 km2 of forest.
clue: A rare, dull-coloured bullfinch in about 6 km2 of native laurel forest on a volcanic island.

place: Glen Catacol, Isle of Arran, Scotland
why_here: It arose by hybridisation on Arran and grows only on a few steep glens there.
fun_fact: It sets seed without pollination, so each tree is basically a clone.
clue: A hybrid that sets seed with no pollination, so each tree is a clone, on steep island slopes.

why_here: Its bill is shaped to pry open the cones of Scotland's native Scots pine forests.
fun_fact: Along with the red grouse, it is one of only two land vertebrates found nowhere but the UK.
clue: Its crossed bill tips pry open cones in cold, ancient pinewoods, and it lives nowhere else.

place: Ball's Pyramid, Lord Howe Island group
why_here: Rats wiped it out on Lord Howe Island around 1920, and the only wild survivors were found clinging to a single shrub patch on a sea stack 23 km offshore.
fun_fact: Nicknamed the 'tree lobster', it was declared extinct for about 80 years before climbers rediscovered a handful on Ball's Pyramid in 2001.
clue: The 'tree lobster' was thought extinct for about 80 years until found on a lone sea stack.

why_here: This flightless rail evolved on predator-free Lord Howe Island and could never leave it.
fun_fact: It was down to about a dozen pairs on mountain summits in the 1970s; after rodent eradication the population passed 1,600 birds by 2024.
clue: A flightless rail once down to about a dozen pairs on misty peaks. Clearing rats saved it.

why_here: Its ancestors reached the tiny volcanic Lord Howe Island and evolved there in isolation; it grows wild nowhere else.
fun_fact: One of the world's most popular houseplants; Queen Victoria kept Kentias in her homes and reportedly had them placed around her coffin.
clue: A world-famous houseplant that grows wild on just one small, old volcanic island.

place: Wollemi National Park, Blue Mountains, NSW
why_here: A relic of Gondwanan forests that survived only in a few damp, sheltered sandstone gorges northwest of Sydney.
fun_fact: Known only from fossils until bushwalkers found it in 1994; fewer than 60 adult trees grow wild and their exact location is kept secret.
clue: A 'living fossil' found by hikers in 1994. Fewer than 60 wild adults hide in damp gorges.

place: Southwest National Park (Port Davey area), Tasmania
why_here: It is a single sterile clone that can only spread by fallen branches rooting, so it has never moved beyond its patch of wet southwest Tasmanian forest.
fun_fact: The whole species is genetically one plant, believed to be at least 43,600 years old, making it one of the oldest living organisms.
clue: The whole species is one sterile clone, thought over 43,000 years old, in wet, cool forest.

why_here: This slow-growing conifer needs the cool, very wet riverbanks of Tasmania's southwest, a Gondwanan refuge found nowhere else.
fun_fact: A stand of genetically identical Huon pines on Mount Read is estimated to be over 10,000 years old.
clue: A slow-growing conifer of cold, soggy riverbanks. One clonal stand may top 10,000 years old.

why_here: An ancient conifer lineage that reached remote Norfolk Island and became a species found wild only there.
fun_fact: Captain Cook hoped its trunks would make ship masts; today it is a common Christmas-tree houseplant worldwide.
clue: Sold worldwide as an indoor Christmas tree, it grows wild only on one tiny, remote island.

place: Mount Pitt, Norfolk Island National Park
why_here: An early-diverging Cyanoramphus parakeet that colonised Norfolk Island and evolved there; it now survives only in the island's national park forest.
fun_fact: Once common, it fell to fewer than 50 birds by the late 1970s.
clue: Once common, this green parakeet fell to fewer than 50 birds in the 1970s, on one small isle.

why_here: Introduced predators eliminated it from the main Chatham Island, leaving it only on small predator-free islets.
fun_fact: Every living black robin descends from one female, 'Old Blue', the last fertile female in 1980.
clue: All alive descend from one female, 'Old Blue', saved on tiny windswept, predator-free islets.

why_here: The only member of its genus, it evolved on the isolated Chatham Islands' coastal shores.
fun_fact: Its huge glossy leaves look nothing like a typical forget-me-not, and it is a prized garden plant worldwide despite its tiny wild range.
clue: Huge glossy leaves and blue flowers on remote, windswept shores. The only one of its genus.

why_here: Its only nesting burrows are in a few forested valleys of southwest Chatham Island, the last place free enough of predators for it to breed.
fun_fact: It was considered extinct for 111 years until it was rediscovered in 1978.
clue: A seabird thought extinct for 111 years until 1978. It nests in burrows in forested valleys.

why_here: It evolved on the remote, treeless subantarctic Antipodes Islands and is found nowhere else.
fun_fact: Unusually for a parrot, it sometimes kills nesting storm petrels in their burrows and eats them.
clue: A meat-eating parrot that sometimes kills petrels in their burrows, on cold, treeless isles.

why_here: A flightless duck that evolved on subantarctic Campbell Island, where there were no ground predators.
fun_fact: Rats wiped it out on Campbell Island; it was rediscovered on tiny Dent Island in 1975 and later returned after rats were eradicated.
clue: A flightless duck wiped out by rats, then found again in 1975 on one tiny islet in cold seas.

why_here: This flightless duck evolved on the subantarctic Auckland Islands and survives on their predator-free islets.
fun_fact: Its wings are so small it cannot fly at all, and it often feeds at night among kelp along the shore.
clue: Too small-winged to fly at all, it often feeds at night among kelp on cold, stormy shores.

place: The Snares, south of New Zealand
why_here: The entire breeding population nests on the tiny forested Snares Islands.
fun_fact: The second egg is much larger than the first and hatches first, so the first-laid chick usually doesn't survive.
clue: A crested penguin whose bigger second egg hatches first. It nests under trees on tiny isles.

why_here: It lives only on the tiny granite Bounty Islands, bare rocks with no plants, about 670 km southeast of New Zealand.
fun_fact: A 2022 drone survey counted about 1,700 birds, a number that has stayed roughly the same since 1978.
clue: About 1,700 live on bare granite rocks without a single plant, far out in a cold, windy sea.

place: Ōkārito forest, West Coast, South Island NZ
why_here: The rarest kiwi survives only in one lowland forest on the South Island's West Coast.
fun_fact: Operation Nest Egg, which hatches eggs in safety and returns chicks to the wild, helped it grow from about 165 adults to around 600.
clue: The rarest of its kind, in one lowland forest. Egg rescues lifted it from about 165 to 600.

why_here: Introduced rats and habitat loss wiped out this ancient frog everywhere except a rocky rat-free island in Cook Strait.
fun_fact: It skips the tadpole stage: embryos develop inside the egg capsule and hatch as tiny froglets.
clue: An ancient frog with no tadpole stage: froglets hatch from eggs on a rocky, rat-free isle.

why_here: It needs the schist rock tors of Central Otago's tussock grasslands, a habitat type it never spread beyond.
fun_fact: New Zealand's largest skink gives birth to live young, usually one to three at a time.
clue: A big, patterned skink of schist rock tors in tussock grassland. It bears live young.

why_here: The whole species breeds only on subantarctic Macquarie Island and its nearby islets.
fun_fact: Millions were boiled down for oil until 1919; the colonies have since recovered to around 850,000 pairs.
clue: Millions were boiled for oil until 1919. About 850,000 pairs now breed on one cold isle.

why_here: A blue-eyed shag that evolved on Macquarie Island and forages only in nearby waters.
fun_fact: Only a few hundred pairs exist, and its numbers fell by about 30% in just three years in the early 2000s.
clue: Only a few hundred pairs of this blue-eyed shag exist, all fishing near one cold, far isle.

why_here: This cushion plant evolved for the windswept, treeless feldmark of Macquarie Island's plateau.
fun_fact: It is the only vascular plant in the island's feldmark habitat and holds the whole ecosystem together.
clue: The only vascular plant on its windswept, treeless plateau, it holds the ecosystem together.

why_here: A pipit that colonised South Georgia, where it was trapped on rat-free offshore islets until a huge rat eradication let it return to the main island.
fun_fact: It is the only songbird in the Antarctic region.
clue: The only songbird in its icy realm, it returned to glacier-lined coasts after a rat purge.

why_here: A resident blue-eyed shag that nests and feeds only around the Kerguelen archipelago, usually within 6 km of shore.
fun_fact: It is the smallest of the blue-eyed shags.
clue: The smallest blue-eyed shag, it rarely feeds more than about 6 km from shore in cold seas.

why_here: Its thick beak is specialised to crack the hard fruits of the island tree Phylica arborea, found in patches on Nightingale and Inaccessible.
fun_fact: It is named after the Australian polar explorer Sir Hubert Wilkins.
clue: A small bird with a massive beak, built to crack the hard fruits of one kind of island tree.

why_here: A thrush lineage that reached the remote Tristan islands and evolved into a separate species there.
fun_fact: It is the largest land predator on Tristan apart from skuas, and will eat seabird eggs and chicks.
clue: A bold thrush that raids seabird eggs and chicks: top land predator on remote volcanic isles.

why_here: The only land songbird on Gough Island evolved there in isolation in the South Atlantic.
fun_fact: Introduced house mice that eat eggs and chicks pushed it to Critically Endangered.
clue: The only land songbird on its wet volcanic isle, where invasive mice eat its eggs and chicks.

place: Ellen Brook, Swan Coastal Plain near Perth
why_here: It depends on seasonal clay-based swamps found only on a thin strip of Perth's Swan Coastal Plain.
fun_fact: It was the first vertebrate moved to a new area specifically because of climate change, about 200 km south.
clue: It needs seasonal clay swamps, and was the first vertebrate relocated due to climate change.

place: Two Peoples Bay, near Albany, WA
why_here: Fire and foxes eliminated it everywhere except one dense heath headland near Albany.
fun_fact: Thought extinct for over a century, it was rediscovered in 1994 in a wallaby trap; it eats mostly underground fungi.
clue: Lost for over a century, it was found again in 1994 in dense coastal heath. It eats fungi.

why_here: A tiny marsupial that evolved on Kangaroo Island and now clings on in the island's western mallee heath.
fun_fact: It is Kangaroo Island's only endemic mammal, and only about 50 may have survived the 2019-20 bushfires.
clue: A mouse-sized marsupial that hunts insects at night in low heath; few survived a huge bushfire.

why_here: It lives only in native grasslands of South Australia's mid-north, sheltering in old spider burrows.
fun_fact: Thought extinct, it was rediscovered in 1992 inside the stomach of a dead brown snake near Burra.
clue: Rediscovered in 1992 inside a dead snake's stomach, it lives in old spider burrows.

why_here: It breeds only in high-altitude sphagnum bogs of the Snowy Mountains between about 1,300 and 1,760 m.
fun_fact: Its bold yellow-and-black stripes advertise toxins it makes itself; fewer than 30 were left in the wild in 2022.
clue: Toxic yellow-and-black stripes in high sphagnum bogs. Fewer than 30 were wild in 2022.

why_here: It is adapted to cold, wet subalpine gullies found only on the Baw Baw plateau.
fun_fact: Its tadpoles never feed or swim freely; they live off egg yolk until they turn into frogs.
clue: Its tadpoles never eat, growing on yolk alone in foam nests in cold, snowy mountain gullies.

why_here: It needs old hollow-bearing mountain ash trees, which survive only in the Central Highlands forests near Melbourne.
fun_fact: Presumed extinct after the 1939 fires, it was rediscovered in 1961; it is Victoria's state faunal emblem.
clue: Thought lost after 1939 fires, found again in 1961, it nests in hollows of old mountain ash.

why_here: It lives only in fast-flowing, oxygen-rich stretches of one river system in southeast Queensland.
fun_fact: Its punk-rock look comes from green algae 'hair', and it can breathe through its cloaca to stay underwater for days.
clue: It has green algae 'hair' and breathes through its rear to stay underwater for days.

why_here: It is restricted to rocky outcrops in rainforest and woodland around the Whitsunday coast.
fun_fact: Science didn't know it existed until 1977, after local farmers reported an odd-looking wallaby.
clue: Unknown to science until 1977, it hops among rocky outcrops in tropical coastal forest.

place: Cardwell region (Tully to Ingham), north Queensland
why_here: It depends on a narrow strip of coastal lowland woodland between Tully and Ingham, most of which has been cleared.
fun_fact: Described in 1886, it went missing for over a century until it was rediscovered in 1989.
clue: A gliding marsupial missing for a century until 1989, in a thin strip of tropical woodland.

why_here: It lives only in the mountain rainforests between the Daintree River and Cooktown, an area of about 70 by 50 km.
fun_fact: It can leap about 9 m between trees and drop 18 m to the ground without injury.
clue: It can leap about 9 m between trees and drop 18 m to the ground unhurt, in tropical hills.

why_here: It is confined to the upland rainforests of the Wet Tropics, centred on the Atherton Tableland.
fun_fact: It is the smallest tree-kangaroo, and its ancestors climbed back into the trees after kangaroos evolved on the ground.
clue: The smallest of its kind. Its ground-living ancestors climbed back into the trees.

why_here: It evolved in the crater lakes and upper rivers of the Atherton Tableland.
fun_fact: It was declared extinct in the wild after predatory fish were illegally added to its lake, then saved via aquarium stocks and nearby streams.
clue: Declared extinct in the wild after predators were put in its crater lake; aquariums saved it.

why_here: A primitive flowering plant that survived only in two small lowland rainforest pockets north and south of Cairns.
fun_fact: Its seeds are poisonous and hold the largest embryo of any flowering plant; it was named after cattle died from eating them.
clue: Its poisonous seeds hold the biggest embryo of any flowering plant, in tiny jungle pockets.

why_here: A Gondwanan rainforest tree that survives in a single creek catchment in the Nightcap Range.
fun_fact: Only about 100 wild trees exist; bushfires burned much of its habitat in 2019-20, but most trees resprouted from their bases.
clue: About 100 wild trees grow by one rainforest creek; most resprouted after 2019-20 wildfires.

place: Southern New Caledonia (Isle of Pines and Blue River)
why_here: It lives only in three small forest areas in southern New Caledonia.
fun_fact: Thought extinct until 1994, it is now one of the world's most popular pet lizards.
clue: Thought extinct until 1994, now one of the most popular pet lizards. It lives in humid forest.

why_here: An ancient flowering-plant lineage that survived only on New Caledonia, an old island that broke off from Gondwana.
fun_fact: It is the sister group of all other flowering plants, which makes it key to understanding how flowers evolved.
clue: Sister to every other flowering plant alive, this shrub survives on one old, humid island.

why_here: It survives only on a few dry-forest islets in western Fiji, where its ancestors are thought to have rafted from the Americas.
fun_fact: Scientists noticed a second population after a crested iguana appeared in the 1980 film The Blue Lagoon.
clue: A banded green iguana whose ancestors may have rafted thousands of km to dry tropical islets.

why_here: It grows only in the high, misty rainforest of Taveuni above 600 m.
fun_fact: It is Fiji's national flower and appears on the Fijian $50 note.
clue: Red-and-white flowers dangle from its vines in misty forest above 600 m, by a crater lake.

why_here: It evolved in the forests of northeastern Fiji and never spread to the other islands.
fun_fact: Males are almost entirely neon orange, with hair-like feathers.
clue: Males are almost entirely neon orange, with odd hair-like feathers, in humid tropical forest.

why_here: It evolved on Fiji's largest island and is found nowhere else.
fun_fact: Its black face mask and yellow-to-orange belly set it apart from the other shining parrots on neighbouring islands.
clue: A big green parrot with a black mask and a yellow-to-orange belly, on one large tropical isle.

why_here: This Samoan endemic is the last survivor of an ancient pigeon lineage on its islands.
fun_fact: Its genus name means 'little dodo', and it is one of the dodo's closest living relatives.
clue: Its genus name means 'little dodo', and it is one of the dodo's closest living relatives.

why_here: It buries its eggs in warm volcanic soil, and its only natural surviving population lives on the volcano island Niuafo'ou.
fun_fact: Parents never sit on their eggs; volcanic heat does the incubating.
clue: Parents never sit on their eggs: they bury them in warm volcanic soil and let heat hatch them.

why_here: A flycatcher that evolved on Rarotonga and survives in its southern forested valleys.
fun_fact: Young birds are orange and turn grey over about four years, which once fooled scientists into thinking they were different species.
clue: Young birds are orange and turn grey over about four years, once fooling scientists.

why_here: It survives only in a few lowland valleys of Tahiti's west coast.
